column6: Moses' older brother and Israel's first high priest, who spoke for Moses before Pharaoh.
The second son of Adam, a keeper of sheep, whose offering was accepted and who was killed by his brother.
Called the father of the faithful; the name was given to him at ninety-nine, replacing Abram.
The first man, formed of the dust of the ground — the name and the word for ground are related in Hebrew.
A herdsman from Tekoa who prophesied against injustice and said he was no prophet by trade.
Peter's brother, and the first of the disciples to bring somebody else to Jesus.
A king of Judah who tore down the idols his fathers had set up.
The eighth son of Jacob, whose name his mother gave because of her own gladness.
Acts gives the translation itself. He vouched for Paul when the church still feared him.
Jacob's youngest son; his mother named him Benoni as she died and his father renamed him.
The kinsman redeemer in the book of Ruth, and an ancestor of David and of Christ.
One of two spies who said Israel could take the land, and who asked for the hill country at eighty-five.
Taken to Babylon as a youth, he served four kings and kept praying with the window open.
The shepherd who killed Goliath, the king who wrote much of the Psalms, called a man after God's own heart.
The high priest who raised Samuel and who mistook Hannah's praying for drunkenness.
The prophet who called down fire on Carmel and heard God afterwards in a still small voice.
Elijah's successor, who asked for a double portion and whose ministry is full of ordinary need met.
He walked with God, and he was not, for God took him — four verses and one of scripture's strangest lines.
Joseph's second son, born in Egypt, who received the greater blessing from Jacob.
Named among the wisest men of his age, and credited with Psalm 89.
A priest carried to Babylon who prophesied to exiles, often by acting things out.
The scribe who led a return from exile and set himself to seek the law, do it, and teach it.
The angel who announced the births of John the Baptist and of Jesus.
Threshing wheat in a winepress when he was greeted as a mighty man of valour.
The son of promise, born to parents past the age for it; his mother laughed when she first heard.
The prophet of the child born, the suffering servant, and wings as eagles.
The name given to Jacob after he wrestled until daybreak, and then to the whole nation.
Born holding his twin's heel; he bought a birthright, stole a blessing, and had his name changed.
The Greek form of Jacob. Two apostles and the writer of the epistle bore it.
One of the patriarchs before the flood, and the father of Enoch.
A believer in Thessalonica who housed Paul and was dragged before the rulers for it.
The weeping prophet, who preached forty years to people who would not listen.
David's father, a Bethlehemite; Isaiah calls the Messiah a rod out of the stem of Jesse.
A prophet whose book promises restored years and the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
Borne by the Baptist and by the apostle Jesus loved, who wrote the Gospel and the Revelation.
He ran from Nineveh, was swallowed and put back on dry land, then sat down angry when the city repented.
Saul's son and heir, who handed David his robe and sword knowing what it cost him.
Sold by his brothers and raised to second in Egypt; ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good.
Moses' successor, who led Israel over the Jordan and made the nation choose at the end of his life.
King at eight; at twenty-six he heard the lost law read and tore his clothes.
Jacob's fourth son, the tribe of David and of Christ, called a lion's whelp in his father's blessing.
The Greek form of Judah. The writer of the short letter near the end of the New Testament.
Jacob's third son and the priestly tribe; also the tax collector who became Matthew.
The physician who travelled with Paul and wrote both a Gospel and the book of Acts.
The last prophet of the Old Testament, who closes it looking forward to one who is coming.
He turned back partway through Paul's first missionary trip and was given a second chance by Barnabas; he wrote the second Gospel.
A tax collector who got up from the table and followed, and who wrote the first Gospel.
The prophet who asked what the LORD requires: to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly.
The archangel named in Daniel, Jude and Revelation, described as standing for God's people.
Drawn out of the Nile, raised in Pharaoh's house, and sent back at eighty to lead a nation out.
The prophet who told David a story about a lamb and then said, thou art the man.
He asked whether any good thing could come out of Nazareth, and was called a man without guile.
He built a boat for years while the ground stayed dry, and God shut the door behind him.
The shortest book in the Old Testament carries this name, borne by more than a dozen men in scripture.
He held the coats at Stephen's stoning, met Christ on the Damascus road, and wrote most of the New Testament.
Jesus gave him the name. He walked on water, denied Christ three times, and preached at Pentecost.
One of the twelve, and also the evangelist who explained Isaiah to an Ethiopian on a desert road.
Jacob's firstborn, who talked his brothers out of killing Joseph.
The strongest of the judges and the least self-controlled; his last act was his greatest.
Given back to God as a boy, he heard his name called in the night and anointed Israel's first two kings.
Israel's first king, head and shoulders above the rest, who lost the throne over partial obedience.
Adam's third son, given, his mother said, in place of Abel.
Paul's companion, singing at midnight in the Philippian jail when the earthquake came.
Jacob's second son, and the old man in the temple who had been promised he would see the Messiah.
Peter's given name, and the name of several other men in the Gospels and Acts.
He asked for an understanding heart instead of riches, built the temple, and wrote much of Proverbs.
Chosen to wait tables, he preached the longest sermon in Acts and was stoned praying for the men doing it.
He would not believe without touching the wounds, and made the highest confession in the Gospel.
Young, often unwell, pastoring a hard church, and the recipient of two letters that read like a father's.
Paul left him in Crete to set things in order, and wrote him a letter about how.
Jacob's tenth son; Isaiah names his territory as the place a great light would be seen.
Jacob's fifth son. Rachel named him, saying God had judged her case and given her a son.
Jacob's sixth son, named for the struggle between Rachel and Leah.
Jacob's seventh son, and also the name of a prophet who advised David.
He tore down the high places and spread an enemy's threatening letter out before the LORD.
A cupbearer who asked leave to rebuild a ruined wall and finished it in fifty-two days.
A grandson of Aaron, remembered for zeal, and the name of two other men in scripture.
A Hittite in David's army, and one of his mighty men, killed to cover up the king's sin.
She rode out to meet an armed David with two hundred loaves and a speech that stopped a massacre.
A prophetess of great age who was in the temple the day Mary and Joseph brought Jesus in.
The title of the Ethiopian queen whose treasurer Philip met on the road to Gaza.
A woman in Corinth whose household told Paul about the divisions in that church.
A believer in Rome who sent greetings in Paul's last letter to Timothy.
An Athenian woman who believed after hearing Paul speak at the Areopagus.
A prophetess and the only woman among Israel's judges, who held court under a palm tree.
The woman who asked Samson four times where his strength lay and sold the answer.
Jacob and Leah's daughter, whose story in Genesis 34 is one of the hardest in the book.
Mary's older cousin, who conceived John the Baptist in old age.
Queen of Persia, who used the position to stop a massacre; the book never names God.
Timothy's mother, named by Paul along with his grandmother Lois for the faith she passed on.
The first woman; Adam named her so because she was the mother of all living.
She prayed for a son so intensely the priest thought her drunk, and gave Samuel back when he came.
One of the women who supported Jesus' ministry and who found the tomb empty.
A believer in Rome greeted by name at the end of Paul's letter.
Abraham's wife after Sarah died, and the mother of six more sons.
One of three daughters born to Job after his restoration, said to be the fairest in the land.
Jacob's first wife, unloved and fruitful; scripture says God saw it and opened her womb.
Timothy's grandmother, credited by Paul with the unfeigned faith that reached her grandson.
A seller of purple whose heart the Lord opened by a river, and the first convert in Europe named.
She complained about the cooking and later made one of the clearest confessions in the Gospels.

column4: Uncertain; the Greek form of Miriam
column6: The mother of Jesus, and the name of several other women in the Gospels including Magdalene.
Saul's daughter and David's first wife, who let him down out of a window to save his life.
Moses' sister, who watched his basket on the Nile and led the women in song after the sea.
She went to Moab full and came back empty, and asked to be called Mara instead.
Ruth's sister-in-law, who kissed Naomi goodbye and went back to her own people.
A tentmaker who, with her husband, took Apollos aside and explained the way of God more perfectly.
The wife Jacob worked fourteen years for, and the mother of Joseph and Benjamin.
She watered ten camels for a stranger and became Isaac's wife on her own decision to go.
The servant girl so glad to hear Peter's voice at the gate that she forgot to open it.
A Moabite widow who would not leave her mother-in-law and ended up in the line of David.
One of the women at the cross and among the first at the tomb on the third morning.
Abraham's wife, who laughed when she overheard she would bear a son at ninety, then bore him.
One of the women named in Luke as supporting Jesus and the twelve out of their own means.
Full of good works; when she died the widows stood around showing Peter the coats she had made.
Borne by three women in scripture, including one named in the genealogy of Christ.
One of Zelophehad's five daughters, who asked for an inheritance and were granted it.
Moses' wife, a daughter of the priest of Midian, who met him at a well in the wilderness.
